claim: Protein crystals were described 150 years ago in eosinophilic inflammatory lesions in humans by Charcot and Vulpian, 1860; Leyden, 1872.
source: Protein crystals have been described already 150 years ago in eosinophilic inflammatory lesions in humans by Charcot and Vulpian, 1860; Leyden, 1872; Aegerter et al., 2021.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to historical work by Charcot and Vulpian (1860) and Leyden (1872), as well as a more recent review (Aegerter et al., 2021).

claim: Spontaneous protein crystallization in vivo remains a rare and largely unsolved scientific enigma.
source: Most proteins can only function properly in the soluble state and spontaneous protein crystallization in vivo remains a rare and largely unsolved scientific enigma (Doye et al., 2004; Schönherr et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scientific literature discussing the rarity and mystery of in vivo protein crystallization.

claim: Protein crystals in mice have been documented almost exclusively in the context of type 2 inflammation, rich in eosinophils, Th2 cells and alternatively activated macrophages.
source: Protein crystals have also been documented in mouse tissues, almost exclusively in the context of type 2 inflammation, rich in eosinophils, T helper 2 (Th2) cells and alternatively activated macrophages (Guo et al., 2000; Hoenerhoff et al., 2006; Takamoto et al., 1997; Shultz et al., 1984; Harbord et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2009; Waern et al., 2010; Poczobutt et al., 2021; Fallon et al., 2001; Rehm et al., 1985; Green, 1942; Murray and Luz, 1990; Yang and Campell, 1964; Feldmesser et al., 2001; Baldán et al., 2008; Huffnagle et al., 1998; Mall et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to multiple studies documenting protein crystals in mouse tissues in the context of type 2 inflammation.

claim: Murine crystals stain brightly with eosin in histochemical stains, consistent with their protein content.
source: Such crystals in mice are colorless, but in histochemical stains they stain brightly with eosin, consistent with their protein content (Fallon et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fallon et al., 2001, describing the staining properties of murine crystals.

claim: Murine crystals were often referred to as eosinophilic crystals before their biochemical nature was elucidated.
source: Before their biochemical nature was elucidated, they were therefore often referred to as eosinophilic crystals (Guo et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2000, describing the historical nomenclature of these crystals.

claim: Murine eosinophilic crystals are frequently observed in aged mice and genetically altered mice on a C57BL/6 or Sv/129 background.
source: These murine crystals are frequently observed in aged mice and genetically altered mice on a C57BL/6 or Sv/129 background, and in the context of eosinophil-rich asthma and parasitic infections (Guo et al., 2000; Roediger et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting the occurrence of crystals in specific mouse strains and conditions.

claim: The principal site of crystal accumulation in mice is in the lung.
source: Although eosinophilic crystals have been documented in the skin, biliary tree, stomach, lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow of mice, it is clear that the principal site of crystal accumulation is in the lung.
evidence: The claim is based on a synthesis of observations from the literature about crystal distribution in various mouse tissues.

claim: Accumulation of eosinophilic crystals was associated with severe lung inflammation called eosinophilic crystalline pneumonia, acidophilic macrophage pneumonia, or crystalline pneumonitis.
source: In several descriptions, accumulation of eosinophilic crystals was associated with severe lung inflammation and the disease was called eosinophilic crystalline pneumonia, acidophilic macrophage pneumonia, or crystalline pneumonitis (Hoenerhoff et al., 2006; Murray and Luz, 1990; Roediger et al., 2015; Henderson et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies describing the association between crystal accumulation and lung inflammation.

claim: Accumulated crystals in mice are variable in size and shape ranging from needle-like crystals to rectangular plates.
source: In histology slides, the accumulated crystals are variable in size and shape ranging from needle-like crystals to rectangular plates (Fallon et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fallon et al., 2001, describing the morphology of crystals in histology.

claim: Murine crystals were incorrectly identified as Charcot-Leyden crystals due to their resemblance to needle-shaped human CLCs.
source: Their resemblance to the needle-shaped human Charcot-Leyden crystals (CLCs) frequently resulted in the incorrect identification of these murine crystals as CLCs (Henderson et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies that incorrectly identified murine crystals as CLCs.

claim: Guo et al. identified the chitinase-like protein Ym1 as the sole protein component of crystals purified from the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of viable motheaten (mev/mev) mice in 2000.
source: However, only in 2000, almost 100 years after they were first described, Guo et al. purified crystals from the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid of viable motheaten (mev/mev) mice and mass spectrometry analysis identified the chitinase-like protein (CLP) Ym1 as the sole protein component (Guo et al., 2000), thereby providing an unambiguous annotation of their content and distinguishing them from CLCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2000, which used mass spectrometry to identify Ym1 as the crystal component.

claim: Human CLCs are comprised of the eosinophil-derived galectin-10 (Gal10) protein.
source: Human CLCs are comprised of the eosinophil-derived galectin-10 (Gal10) protein, which is not encoded in the mouse genome (Leonidas et al., 1995; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing the composition of human CLCs.

claim: Galectin-10 is not encoded in the mouse genome.
source: Human CLCs are comprised of the eosinophil-derived galectin-10 (Gal10) protein, which is not encoded in the mouse genome (Leonidas et al., 1995; Swaminathan et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies and is based on genomic knowledge.

claim: Ym1 is mainly produced by alveolar macrophages, alternatively activated 'M2' macrophages, neutrophils and a subset of circulating pro-repair monocytes.
source: Ym1 is mainly produced by alveolar macrophages, alternatively activated 'M2' macrophages, neutrophils and a subset of circulating pro-repair monocytes (Raes et al., 2002; Ikeda et al., 2018; Aegerter et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies identifying the cellular sources of Ym1.

claim: Pseudo-CLCs in hyaline gastric lesions of aged 129S4/SvJae and B6,129 CYP1A2 null mice consist of the closely related CLP Ym2.
source: In hyaline gastric lesions of aged 129S4/SvJae and B6,129 CYP1A2 null mice, pseudo-CLCs were found to consist of the closely related CLP Ym2, which is a protein mainly made by epithelial cells under the influence of IL-13 (Fallon et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 1999; Ward et al., 2001; Parkinson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies identifying Ym2 as the component of pseudo-CLCs in specific mouse models.

claim: Ym2 is a protein mainly made by epithelial cells under the influence of IL-13.
source: In hyaline gastric lesions of aged 129S4/SvJae and B6,129 CYP1A2 null mice, pseudo-CLCs were found to consist of the closely related CLP Ym2, which is a protein mainly made by epithelial cells under the influence of IL-13 (Fallon et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 1999; Ward et al., 2001; Parkinson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing Ym2 production.

claim: Ym1 (encoded by the Chil3 gene) and Ym2 (encoded by the Chil4 gene) are chitinase-like proteins belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 18 (GH18).
source: Ym1 (encoded by the Chil3 gene) and Ym2 (encoded by the Chil4 gene) are CLPs belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 18 (GH18) and are unique to mice, with no known human orthologues (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Dyken and Locksley, 2018, which characterizes these proteins.

claim: Ym1 and Ym2 are unique to mice, with no known human orthologues.
source: Ym1 (encoded by the Chil3 gene) and Ym2 (encoded by the Chil4 gene) are CLPs belonging to the glycoside hydrolase family 18 (GH18) and are unique to mice, with no known human orthologues (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Van Dyken and Locksley, 2018, and reflects genomic knowledge.

claim: The potential receptors and natural binding partners of Ym1 and Ym2 are largely unknown.
source: Their potential receptors and natural binding partners are largely unknown, as are the exact functions of these still very enigmatic proteins.
evidence: The claim reflects the current state of knowledge about Ym1 and Ym2.

claim: Recombinant Gal10 crystals produced in vitro showed crystal packing and structure identical to CLCs derived from patient mucus.
source: We previously reported that recombinant Gal10 crystals produced in vitro showed crystal packing and structure identical to CLCs derived from patient mucus.
evidence: The claim refers to previous work by the authors, which would have included crystallographic data.

claim: When administered to the airways of mice, Gal10 crystals stimulated innate and adaptive immunity and acted as a type 2 adjuvant.
source: When administered to the airways of mice, Gal10 crystals stimulated innate and adaptive immunity and acted as a type 2 adjuvant (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019, which reported experimental findings.

claim: Mice do not encode the LGALS10 gene.
source: Since mice do not encode the LGALS10 gene, Gal10 has the potential to act as a neo-antigen in this setting.
evidence: The claim is based on genomic knowledge about mice.

claim: Gal10 has the potential to act as a neo-antigen in mice.
source: Since mice do not encode the LGALS10 gene, Gal10 has the potential to act as a neo-antigen in this setting.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the absence of the LGALS10 gene in mice.

claim: Recombinant in vitro made Ym1 and Ym2 crystals were structurally similar to crystals isolated from mice and to each other.
source: We showed that recombinant in vitro made Ym1 and Ym2 crystals were structurally similar to crystals isolated from mice and to each other, and when administered to the airways of mice, crystalline Ym1, but not soluble Ym1 protein stimulated innate and adaptive immunity and acted as an adjuvant for Th2 driven eosinophilic airway inflammation and immunoglobulin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: When administered to the airways of mice, crystalline Ym1, but not soluble Ym1 protein stimulated innate and adaptive immunity.
source: We showed that recombinant in vitro made Ym1 and Ym2 crystals were structurally similar to crystals isolated from mice and to each other, and when administered to the airways of mice, crystalline Ym1, but not soluble Ym1 protein stimulated innate and adaptive immunity and acted as an adjuvant for Th2 driven eosinophilic airway inflammation and immunoglobulin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-5.

claim: Crystalline Ym1 acted as an adjuvant for Th2 driven eosinophilic airway inflammation and immunoglobulin secretion.
source: We showed that recombinant in vitro made Ym1 and Ym2 crystals were structurally similar to crystals isolated from mice and to each other, and when administered to the airways of mice, crystalline Ym1, but not soluble Ym1 protein stimulated innate and adaptive immunity and acted as an adjuvant for Th2 driven eosinophilic airway inflammation and immunoglobulin secretion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Crystals obtained from the BAL fluid of mev/mev mice were Ym1 crystals.
source: Crystallographic studies using microfocus synchrotron X-rays showed that the crystals obtained from the BAL fluid of mev/mev mice were Ym1 crystals, in accordance with a previous report (Guo et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data and a citation to Guo et al., 2000.

claim: Crystals obtained from the BAL fluid of C57BL/6J-Tg(CAG-Gal10)Bla mice are Ym2 crystals.
source: We had hypothesized that the crystals obtained from the BAL fluid of C57BL/6J-Tg(CAG-Gal10)Bla mice were CLCs containing Gal10. However, crystallographic characterization of these crystals revealed that they are Ym2 crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recombinant Ym1 and Ym2 protein were produced in FreeStyle 293 F cells.
source: In parallel, we produced recombinant Ym1 and Ym2 protein in FreeStyle 293 F cells.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Spontaneous crystallization of Ym1 and Ym2 was aided by low pH and low temperature (4 °C).
source: Spontaneous crystallization was aided by low pH and low temperature (4 °C) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim describes experimental conditions and is supported by images in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystals and recombinant Ym1 crystals were crystallographically equivalent, sharing the same monoclinic space group (P21) and unit-cell parameters.
source: Native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystals and recombinant Ym1 crystals (Figure 1C) as well as native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystals and recombinant Ym2 crystals (Figure 1D) were crystallographically equivalent, sharing the same monoclinic space group (P21) and unit-cell parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystals and recombinant Ym2 crystals were crystallographically equivalent, sharing the same monoclinic space group (P21) and unit-cell parameters.
source: Native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystals and recombinant Ym1 crystals (Figure 1C) as well as native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystals and recombinant Ym2 crystals (Figure 1D) were crystallographically equivalent, sharing the same monoclinic space group (P21) and unit-cell parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: A native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystal and a native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystal are structurally similar to each other.
source: Moreover, X-ray crystallographic studies showed that a native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystal and a native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystal are structurally similar to each other, which is not so surprisingly as Ym1 (Chil3) and Ym2 (Chil4) are two closely related proteins sharing 95% nucleotide sequence identity and 91% amino acid sequence identity (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 1E, F, and G.

claim: Ym1 (Chil3) and Ym2 (Chil4) share 95% nucleotide sequence identity and 91% amino acid sequence identity.
source: Moreover, X-ray crystallographic studies showed that a native in vivo isolated Ym1 crystal and a native in vivo isolated Ym2 crystal are structurally similar to each other, which is not so surprisingly as Ym1 (Chil3) and Ym2 (Chil4) are two closely related proteins sharing 95% nucleotide sequence identity and 91% amino acid sequence identity (Figure 1E, F and G).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence comparison, which is established knowledge.

claim: After 6 and 24 hr, there was a prominent influx of Ly6C+ monocytes and eosinophils into the airways of mice receiving Ym1 crystals but not in those receiving soluble Ym1 or PBS.
source: After 6 and 24 hr, there was a prominent influx of Ly6C+ monocytes and eosinophils into the airways of mice receiving Ym1 crystals but not in those receiving soluble Ym1 or PBS.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Neutrophil numbers were increased in the Ym1 crystal group, but this failed to reach statistical significance.
source: Neutrophil numbers were also increased in the Ym1 crystal group, but this failed to reach statistical significance (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The cellular influx induced by Ym1 crystals was accompanied by the production of the innate pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNFα in BAL fluid.
source: This influx was accompanied by the production of the innate pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNFα in BAL fluid (Figure 2C) and the inflammasome-dependent cytokine IL-1β and the alarmin IL-33 in lung tissue only in the group receiving crystalline Ym1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The inflammasome-dependent cytokine IL-1β and the alarmin IL-33 were produced in lung tissue only in the group receiving crystalline Ym1.
source: This influx was accompanied by the production of the innate pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNFα in BAL fluid (Figure 2C) and the inflammasome-dependent cytokine IL-1β and the alarmin IL-33 in lung tissue only in the group receiving crystalline Ym1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and the eosinophil chemoattractant CCL24 (Eotaxin-2) were found enhanced in lung tissue of the crystal-treated group.
source: The monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and the eosinophil chemoattractant CCL24 (Eotaxin-2) were found enhanced in lung tissue of the crystal-treated group (Figure 2E), particularly at early time points, suggesting these paracrine signals were driving the cellular influx induced by crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: CCL2 and CCL24 were enhanced particularly at early time points, suggesting these paracrine signals were driving the cellular influx induced by crystals.
source: The monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and the eosinophil chemoattractant CCL24 (Eotaxin-2) were found enhanced in lung tissue of the crystal-treated group (Figure 2E), particularly at early time points, suggesting these paracrine signals were driving the cellular influx induced by crystals.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the timing of chemokine production and cellular influx data.

claim: The i.t. injected pre-formed Ym1 crystals were still present as intact crystals after 6 and 24 hr.
source: The results clearly showed that the i.t. injected pre-formed Ym1 crystals were still present as intact crystals after 6 and 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by ImageStream data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Soluble Ym1 protein crystallized in vivo after i.t. injection, with crystals being clearly detectable after 6 hr and accumulating further after 24 hr.
source: The soluble Ym1 protein indeed crystallized in vivo, with crystals being clearly detectable after 6 hr and accumulating further after 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by ImageStream data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: The crystals formed in vivo after i.t. injection of soluble Ym1 were plate-like, but had a less uniform distribution and were smaller in size than the i.t. injected Ym1 crystals.
source: The crystals formed in vivo after i.t. injection of soluble Ym1 were also plate-like, but had a less uniform distribution and were smaller in size than the i.t. injected Ym1 crystals (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ImageStream data presented in Figure 2F.

claim: The total number of crystals found in the BAL pellet of soluble Ym1 treated mice (266 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets) was lower than in the BAL pellet of Ym1 crystal treated mice (1355 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets).
source: The total number of crystals found in the BAL pellet of soluble Ym1 treated mice (266 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets) was lower than in the BAL pellet of Ym1 crystal treated mice (1355 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets), potentially explaining why the soluble Ym1 group had less inflammation compared with the group receiving pre-formed Ym1 crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative ImageStream data.

claim: The lower number of crystals in the soluble Ym1 group potentially explains why this group had less inflammation compared with the group receiving pre-formed Ym1 crystals.
source: The total number of crystals found in the BAL pellet of soluble Ym1 treated mice (266 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets) was lower than in the BAL pellet of Ym1 crystal treated mice (1355 crystals in 5 pooled BAL pellets), potentially explaining why the soluble Ym1 group had less inflammation compared with the group receiving pre-formed Ym1 crystals.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between crystal number and inflammation.

claim: IL-1β, IL-33, IL-6, and TNFα in the lungs can activate antigen presenting cells.
source: We next studied whether innate immunity triggered by Ym1 crystals was accompanied by the induction of adaptive immunity, particularly since IL-1β, IL-33, IL-6, and TNFα in the lungs can activate antigen presenting cells (Lambrecht and Hammad, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lambrecht and Hammad, 2012.

claim: Airway DCs bridge innate and adaptive immunity.
source: Airway DCs bridge innate and adaptive immunity and can be activated by recombinant Gal10 crystals and monosodium urate (MSU) crystals (Persson et al., 2019; Kool et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating DC activation by crystals.

claim: Airway DCs can be activated by recombinant Gal10 crystals and monosodium urate (MSU) crystals.
source: Airway DCs bridge innate and adaptive immunity and can be activated by recombinant Gal10 crystals and monosodium urate (MSU) crystals (Persson et al., 2019; Kool et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Persson et al., 2019 and Kool et al., 2011.

claim: In mice given Ym1 crystals in the presence of fluorescently labeled OVA antigen, there was a clear increase in the number of total lung-draining mLN CD26+CD88-CD11c+CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs).
source: In mice given Ym1 crystals in the presence of fluorescently labeled OVA antigen (Figure 3B), there was a clear increase in the number of total lung-draining mLN CD26+CD88-CD11c+CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs), numerically mainly caused by an increase in the number of CD172+ cDC2, compared with mice receiving PBS or soluble Ym1, although XCR1+ cDC1s also clearly reacted to the crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase in cDCs was numerically mainly caused by an increase in the number of CD172+ cDC2.
source: In mice given Ym1 crystals in the presence of fluorescently labeled OVA antigen (Figure 3B), there was a clear increase in the number of total lung-draining mLN CD26+CD88-CD11c+CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs), numerically mainly caused by an increase in the number of CD172+ cDC2, compared with mice receiving PBS or soluble Ym1, although XCR1+ cDC1s also clearly reacted to the crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: XCR1+ cDC1s also clearly reacted to the Ym1 crystals.
source: In mice given Ym1 crystals in the presence of fluorescently labeled OVA antigen (Figure 3B), there was a clear increase in the number of total lung-draining mLN CD26+CD88-CD11c+CD64- conventional DCs (cDCs), numerically mainly caused by an increase in the number of CD172+ cDC2, compared with mice receiving PBS or soluble Ym1, although XCR1+ cDC1s also clearly reacted to the crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: There was an increase in the number of mLN CD88+CD11b+ monocytes that expressed intermediate levels of CD11c induced by Ym1 crystals.
source: There was also an increase in the number of mLN CD88+CD11b+ monocytes that expressed intermediate levels of CD11c induced by crystals (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Exposure to crystalline Ym1 led to an increase in cDC1s, cDC2s and monocytes taking up the co-administered fluorescent OVA antigen.
source: Not surprisingly, the exposure to crystalline Ym1 also led to an increase in cDC1s, cDC2s and monocytes taking up the co-administered fluorescent OVA antigen (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Exposure to soluble Ym1 and Ym1 crystals induced an upregulation of the costimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86.
source: Exposure to soluble Ym1 and Ym1 crystals also induced an upregulation of the costimulatory molecules CD80 (data not shown) and CD86, and this effect was most pronounced with crystalline Ym1, and particularly in cDCs that were also taking up fluorescent OVA (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: The upregulation of CD86 was most pronounced with crystalline Ym1, and particularly in cDCs that were also taking up fluorescent OVA.
source: Exposure to soluble Ym1 and Ym1 crystals also induced an upregulation of the costimulatory molecules CD80 (data not shown) and CD86, and this effect was most pronounced with crystalline Ym1, and particularly in cDCs that were also taking up fluorescent OVA (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: When innocuous OVA was injected i.t. together with Ym1 crystals, the adoptively transferred OT-II KN2 T cells showed increased proliferation 4 days later in the mLNs.
source: When innocuous OVA was injected i.t. together with Ym1 crystals, the adoptively transferred OT-II KN2 T cells showed increased proliferation 4 days (Figure 4B) and 7 days (data not shown) later in the mLNs, an effect absent when OVA was given with soluble Ym1.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The increased proliferation of OT-II KN2 T cells was absent when OVA was given with soluble Ym1.
source: When innocuous OVA was injected i.t. together with Ym1 crystals, the adoptively transferred OT-II KN2 T cells showed increased proliferation 4 days (Figure 4B) and 7 days (data not shown) later in the mLNs, an effect absent when OVA was given with soluble Ym1.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Ym1 crystals led to the accumulation of higher numbers of OT-II T cells and Th2 polarizing KN2 +OT II T cells in the mLNs 4 days after the i.t. administration.
source: This led to the accumulation of higher numbers of OT-II T cells and Th2 polarizing KN2 +OT II T cells in the mLNs 4 days (Figure 4C) and 7 days (Figure 4D) after the i.t. administration.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: After 7 days, divided OT-II T cells and KN2 +OT II T cells could be found in the lungs of mice receiving OVA mixed with Ym1 crystals.
source: After 7 days, divided OT-II T cells and KN2 +OT II T cells could also be found in the lungs of mice receiving OVA mixed with Ym1 crystals (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: The OT-II T cells found in the lungs lost CD62L expression while expressing CD44, showing they had become effector cells.
source: These cells lost CD62L expression while expressing CD44, showing they had become effector cells (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on flow cytometry data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Mice sensitized i.t. with OVA mixed with Ym1 crystals exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells.
source: These mice exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells (Figure 5B), a higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures (Figure 5C) and a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response, a hallmark of type 2 immunity, most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Mice sensitized with OVA and Ym1 crystals showed higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures.
source: These mice exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells (Figure 5B), a higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures (Figure 5C) and a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response, a hallmark of type 2 immunity, most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Mice sensitized with OVA and Ym1 crystals showed a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response.
source: These mice exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells (Figure 5B), a higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures (Figure 5C) and a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response, a hallmark of type 2 immunity, most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: OVA-specific IgG1 is a hallmark of type 2 immunity.
source: These mice exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells (Figure 5B), a higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures (Figure 5C) and a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response, a hallmark of type 2 immunity, most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on established immunological knowledge.

claim: The OVA-specific IgG1 response was most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells.
source: These mice exhibited airway inflammation characterized by an influx of eosinophils, B cells and T cells (Figure 5B), a higher production of the type 2 cytokines IL-5, IL-10, and IL-13 in the supernatants of mLN restimulation cultures (Figure 5C) and a robust OVA-specific IgG1 response, a hallmark of type 2 immunity, most likely driven by enhanced IL-4 production in Th2 or TFH cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on immunological knowledge about IgG1 class switching.

claim: The induction of allergic type 2 inflammation was specifically related to the crystalline state of Ym1.
source: Thus, the induction of allergic type 2 inflammation was specifically related to the crystalline state of Ym1.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing crystalline and soluble Ym1.

claim: Recombinant Gal10 crystals mounted high titers of Gal10-specific IgG1 antibodies when used as adjuvant.
source: In contrast to recombinant Gal10 crystals, which mounted high titers of Gal10-specific IgG1 antibodies when used as adjuvant in the same experimental set-up (Persson et al., 2019), Ym1 crystals did not elicit an antibody response directed to Ym1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019.

claim: Ym1 crystals did not elicit an antibody response directed to Ym1 in the OVA-induced asthma model.
source: In contrast to recombinant Gal10 crystals, which mounted high titers of Gal10-specific IgG1 antibodies when used as adjuvant in the same experimental set-up (Persson et al., 2019), Ym1 crystals did not elicit an antibody response directed to Ym1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: When mice received repetitive injections of Ym1 crystals via i.p. injection, high titers of Ym1-specific IgM were detected.
source: However, when mice received repetitive injections of Ym1 crystals in a different set-up via i.p. injection (Figure 5F), high titers of Ym1-specific IgM were detected (Figure 5G), suggesting that Ym1 crystals can trigger an autoimmune response or elicit a recall response from natural IgM antibody producing peritoneal B cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: Ym1 crystals can trigger an autoimmune response or elicit a recall response from natural IgM antibody producing peritoneal B cells.
source: However, when mice received repetitive injections of Ym1 crystals in a different set-up via i.p. injection (Figure 5F), high titers of Ym1-specific IgM were detected (Figure 5G), suggesting that Ym1 crystals can trigger an autoimmune response or elicit a recall response from natural IgM antibody producing peritoneal B cells.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the detection of Ym1-specific IgM.

claim: Ym1 and Ym2 are among the most strongly induced proteins in the airways of mice after allergen exposure.
source: Ym1 and Ym2 are among the most strongly induced proteins in the airways of mice after allergen exposure (Jeong et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2007; Wong and Zhao, 2008) and both proteins readily form pseudo-CLCs in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting Ym1 and Ym2 induction after allergen exposure.

claim: Both Ym1 and Ym2 proteins readily form pseudo-CLCs in vivo.
source: Ym1 and Ym2 are among the most strongly induced proteins in the airways of mice after allergen exposure (Jeong et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2007; Wong and Zhao, 2008) and both proteins readily form pseudo-CLCs in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the literature and the current study.

claim: Ym1 and Ym2 have become markers of type 2 inflammation.
source: As a result, Ym1 and Ym2 have become markers of type 2 inflammation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The phase transition of soluble Ym1/Ym2 to crystalline pseudo-CLC states leads to profound immunostimulatory effects on innate and adaptive type 2 immunity.
source: Here we show by ex vivo X-ray crystallography that Ym2 also crystallizes in vivo and that the phase transition of soluble Ym1/Ym2 to crystalline pseudo-CLC states leads to profound immunostimulatory effects on innate and adaptive type 2 immunity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sutherland and colleagues showed that vector-based overexpression of Ym1 or Ym2 in the lung increased the number of neutrophils in the BAL fluid.
source: Sutherland and colleagues have shown that vector-based overexpression of Ym1 or Ym2 in the lung increased the number of neutrophils in the BAL fluid (Sutherland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sutherland et al., 2014.

claim: It is unclear whether the effects observed by Sutherland et al. were due to the crystalline or soluble state of Ym1/2.
source: Whether these observed effects were due to the crystalline or soluble state of Ym1/2 remains unclear from these studies.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: Several attempts to produce crystallization-deficient soluble Ym1 or Ym2 muteins failed.
source: So far, several attempts to produce crystallization-deficient soluble Ym1 or Ym2 muteins failed, despite the fact that this was feasible for the CLC protein Gal10 (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes unsuccessful experimental attempts by the authors.

claim: Production of crystallization-deficient muteins was feasible for the CLC protein Gal10.
source: So far, several attempts to produce crystallization-deficient soluble Ym1 or Ym2 muteins failed, despite the fact that this was feasible for the CLC protein Gal10 (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019.

claim: Anti-Gal10 antibodies were able to dissolve pre-existing CLCs and to inhibit key features of airway CLC crystallopathy in a humanized mouse model of asthma.
source: In Persson et al., 2019, we produced anti-Gal10 antibodies able to dissolve pre-existing CLCs and to inhibit key features of airway CLC crystallopathy in a humanized mouse model of asthma (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019.

claim: Blocking antibodies directed against Ym1/2 suppressed neutrophilic inflammation in the lungs of asthmatic mice and helminth-infected mice.
source: Sutherland and colleagues have shown that blocking antibodies directed against Ym1/2 suppressed neutrophilic inflammation in the lungs of asthmatic mice and helminth-infected mice (Persson et al., 2019; Sutherland et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Persson et al., 2019 and Sutherland et al., 2014.

claim: It is unclear if anti-Ym1/2 antibodies suppressed lung neutrophilia by dissolving possible Ym1/2 pseudo-CLCs.
source: However, it is unclear if these anti-Ym1/2 antibodies used suppressed lung neutrophilia by dissolving possible Ym1/2 pseudo-CLCs.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism of action of anti-Ym1/2 antibodies.

claim: Ym1 crystals induced an auto-antibody response of the IgM isotype.
source: We also observed that Ym1 crystals induced an auto-antibody response of the IgM isotype, suggesting intrinsic adjuvant activity in the crystalline state of Ym1.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data presented in Figure 5G.

claim: The IgM response to Ym1 crystals suggests intrinsic adjuvant activity in the crystalline state of Ym1.
source: We also observed that Ym1 crystals induced an auto-antibody response of the IgM isotype, suggesting intrinsic adjuvant activity in the crystalline state of Ym1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed IgM response.

claim: Antibodies to Ym1/2 have been described to occur in a model of incipient neoplasia in mice overexpressing the Epstein Barr virus oncogene LMP1 in the skin.
source: Antibodies to Ym1/2 have been described to occur also in a model of incipient neoplasia in mice overexpressing the Epstein Barr virus oncogene LMP1 in the skin, leading to chronic inflammation (Qureshi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qureshi et al., 2011.

claim: It is unclear if induction of auto-antibodies to Ym1/2 in LMP1-overexpressing mice would be the result of spontaneous crystallization of Ym1/2 in the skin.
source: However, it is unclear if induction of such auto-antibodies to Ym1/2 would be the result of spontaneous crystallization of Ym1/2 in the skin of these mice.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the mechanism of auto-antibody induction.

claim: Recognition of endogenously produced MSU or cholesterol crystals by IgM has been described previously.
source: Recognition of endogenously produced MSU or cholesterol crystals by IgM has been described previously (Pilely et al., 2016; Kanevets et al., 2009), and in the case of MSU, it was even proposed that IgM is required to turn soluble uric acid (UA) into an immunostimulatory adjuvant (Kanevets et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pilely et al., 2016 and Kanevets et al., 2009.

claim: It was proposed that IgM is required to turn soluble uric acid (UA) into an immunostimulatory adjuvant.
source: Recognition of endogenously produced MSU or cholesterol crystals by IgM has been described previously (Pilely et al., 2016; Kanevets et al., 2009), and in the case of MSU, it was even proposed that IgM is required to turn soluble uric acid (UA) into an immunostimulatory adjuvant (Kanevets et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kanevets et al., 2009.

claim: Future studies will have to establish if IgM contributes to the adjuvanticity of Ym1 crystals or facilitates the transition of soluble to crystalline Ym1.
source: Future studies will have to establish if IgM contributes in some way to the adjuvanticity of Ym1 crystals or facilitates the transition of soluble to crystalline Ym1.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Native in vivo grown Ym1 crystals are structurally similar to native in vivo grown Ym2 crystals.
source: Ym1 (Chil3) and Ym2 (Chil4) share 95% nucleotide sequence identity and 91% amino acid sequence identity and we now show here that native in vivo grown Ym1 crystals are structurally similar to native in vivo grown Ym2 crystals.
evidence: The claim is supported by crystallographic data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Ym2 crystals most likely will stimulate innate and adaptive immunity and act as a type 2 adjuvant, similar to Ym1 crystals.
source: Given these similarities, we assume that Ym2 crystals most likely will stimulate innate and adaptive immunity and act as a type 2 adjuvant, similar to Ym1 crystals, although we did not formally demonstrate this experimentally.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on structural similarity between Ym1 and Ym2 crystals.

claim: Ym1 is mainly expressed by macrophages, neutrophils and a subset of circulating pro-repair monocytes, while Ym2 is produced by lung epithelial cells.
source: However, Ym1 is mainly expressed by macrophages, neutrophils and a subset of circulating pro-repair monocytes, while Ym2 is produced by lung epithelial cells, which could have discrete context dependent benefits.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the cellular sources of Ym1 and Ym2.

claim: The different cellular sources of Ym1 and Ym2 could have discrete context dependent benefits.
source: However, Ym1 is mainly expressed by macrophages, neutrophils and a subset of circulating pro-repair monocytes, while Ym2 is produced by lung epithelial cells, which could have discrete context dependent benefits.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the functional significance of different cellular sources.

claim: Understanding the requirements for protein crystal formation during type 2 immunity will help to better understand if targeting CLCs in human asthma and CRSwNPs would be of value.
source: Understanding the requirements for protein crystal formation during type 2 immunity, studying the mechanisms whereby protein crystals stimulate type 2 immunity and having the proper tools to be able to distinguish between the soluble and the crystalline state will help us to better understand if targeting CLCs in human asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNPs) would be of value.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the translational implications of the research.

claim: CLCs and pseudo-CLCs are almost exclusively found in eosinophilic airway inflammation across many species.
source: Since CLCs and pseudo-CLCs are almost exclusively found in eosinophilic airway inflammation across many species, and share many biological effects, it appears that protein crystallization is a more generalized feature of type 2 immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from the literature and the current study.

claim: CLCs and pseudo-CLCs share many biological effects.
source: Since CLCs and pseudo-CLCs are almost exclusively found in eosinophilic airway inflammation across many species, and share many biological effects, it appears that protein crystallization is a more generalized feature of type 2 immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on the comparison of Gal10 and Ym1 crystal effects in this and previous studies.

claim: Protein crystallization is a more generalized feature of type 2 immunity.
source: Since CLCs and pseudo-CLCs are almost exclusively found in eosinophilic airway inflammation across many species, and share many biological effects, it appears that protein crystallization is a more generalized feature of type 2 immunity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the widespread occurrence of protein crystals in type 2 immunity.

claim: The cellular influx and production of cytokines and chemokines observed after recombinant Ym1 crystal injection was also observed with recombinant Gal10 crystals.
source: The cellular influx and production of several cytokines and chemokines we observed after recombinant Ym1 crystal injection was also observed in earlier work where recombinant Gal10 crystals were injected into the lung of mice (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019.

claim: Gal10 crystals were able to recruit and activate DCs, activate cellular and humoral adaptive immune responses and act as type 2 adjuvants.
source: Besides triggering innate immunity, Gal10 crystals, just like Ym1 crystals were able to recruit and activate DCs, activate cellular and humoral adaptive immune responses and act as type 2 adjuvants (Persson et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Persson et al., 2019.

claim: Organic non-proteinaceous crystals such as MSU crystals and crystalline alum were able to recruit and activate DCs and act as type 2 adjuvants.
source: Besides, not only protein crystals, but also organic non-proteinaceous crystals such as MSU crystals and crystalline alum were able to recruit and activate DCs and act as type 2 adjuvants (Kool et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2014), suggesting that promotion of type 2 response is a generic response to crystals of different chemical composition.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kool et al., 2011 and Williams et al., 2014.

claim: Promotion of type 2 response is a generic response to crystals of different chemical composition.
source: Besides, not only protein crystals, but also organic non-proteinaceous crystals such as MSU crystals and crystalline alum were able to recruit and activate DCs and act as type 2 adjuvants (Kool et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2014), suggesting that promotion of type 2 response is a generic response to crystals of different chemical composition.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that various types of crystals promote type 2 responses.

claim: The convergent evolution of CLCs and pseudo-CLCs as protein crystals in type 2 immunity strongly suggests a selective evolutionary advantage of these protein crystals in the enhancement of type 2-driven immune responses.
source: The convergent evolution of CLCs and pseudo-CLCs as protein crystals in type 2 immunity strongly suggests a selective evolutionary advantage of these protein crystals in the enhancement of type 2-driven immune responses.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of protein crystallization in type 2 immunity.
